request: We'd like managers to edit and re-approve documents after they've already been signed.

success_metrics.value: Not stated. A plausible measure is that a manager can issue a corrected version without admin help, and nobody acts on a superseded version.

payer.value: Existing client of the platform; a feature for the platform, not a standalone product.

actors.value: Managers edit and trigger re-approval. Unknown: any manager or only the document's owner, who approves the new version (the same manager is a segregation-of-duties problem), and who the original signatories are.

workflow.value: Proposed: signed v1 (current) -> manager drafts v2 -> review/approval circuit -> re-signature -> v2 published, v1 stamped superseded. integrations.value: Signature is an event other modules subscribe to; a second signature may re-trigger downstream automation (e.g. invoicing, contract activation). Notification recipients and the e-signature provider are unknown.

permissions.value: A new right 'create a new version of a signed document' for managers, separate from the right to approve. Scope (own team/entity/classification) is unknown. Classification determines who sees v2 and the pending draft.

config_vs_custom.value: Unknown whether the re-approval circuit and who may edit is the same for all clients or configurable per client.
config_vs_custom.evidence: Context: approval circuits and rights are client-specific on this platform.

reporting.value: A full audit trail is needed: who changed what, previous vs new version, who re-approved and when, and a view of the version history. acceptance.value: Not defined. Proposed scenarios: a manager issues v2, v1 stays retrievable and stamped superseded, v2 requires re-approval before becoming current, and the audit shows the full chain.

risks.value: People may act on the wrong version (approved vs current), prior signatures may be wrongly treated as still covering v2, and downstream automation may fire twice. A gradual rollout starting with one document type would limit exposure.
risks.evidence: Deduced from the context card traps.

challenges.headline: Editing a signed document
challenges.premise: Managers 'edit' a document that has already been signed.
challenges.alternative: Treat every change as a new version that supersedes the signed one. The signed version stays frozen, retrievable and referenceable, and the manager works on a draft of the successor.
challenges.consequence: An in-place edit would break the validity of existing signatures, destroy the evidence of what was signed, and leave citations and prior approvals pointing at content that no longer exists.
challenges.recommendation: Get the client's agreement that the signed version is never modified before any design starts.

challenges.headline: Re-approval is not re-signature
challenges.premise: Sending the change back through approval is enough to make it valid.
challenges.alternative: Decide separately whether the new version needs only internal re-approval or also fresh signatures from the original signatories. Prior signatures do not automatically cover the new content.
challenges.consequence: Treating them as the same either leaves a version in force that nobody with signing authority has signed, or adds an e-signature round that the business did not need.
challenges.recommendation: Ask which document types need new signatures and which only need internal re-approval, then build each path explicitly.

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A new capability is needed for managers to amend signed documents.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has versioning, approval circuits and publication. Opening the existing supersession path to a manager role, with configured circuits, may deliver most of the request.
challenges.consequence: Building a separate amendment feature duplicates the approval circuits and creates a second way to change documents, which is more to maintain and more to audit.
challenges.recommendation: Review what is already available or switched off, including the e-signature provider's re-sign capability, before estimating any new build.

page.title: Changing signed documents safely
page.recommendation: Decide whether managers may change a signed document by issuing a new version that supersedes it, rather than editing the signed one. We recommend this approach, reusing the platform's existing versioning and approval circuits, and piloting it on one document type before extending it.
page.why: A signed version is the evidence of what was agreed, so changing it in place would undermine the signatures and the history. A successor version keeps the original retrievable and lets the change go through its own approval. The platform already offers versioning, approval circuits and publication, so much of this may be configuration and a new manager right rather than a new build. Your request names re-approval, but a change to signed content may also need fresh signatures, and that is the point that most changes the build.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is in the supersession rules and the handling of re-signature. The risk that matters most is people acting on the wrong version, or a repeated signature firing downstream actions such as invoicing a second time. A pilot on one document type limits both.

open.question: Can you give a real example of a signed document that had to change, and how it was handled?
open.would_change: If changes are mostly typo corrections, a lighter correction path could replace the full re-approval flow; if they are commercial changes, re-signature is likely required.

open.question: Do you agree that the signed version is never modified, and that an edit always creates a new version that goes through approval? Are there document types that must never be changed after signature, or rules that differ by client or document type?
open.would_change: If in-place correction of signed documents is expected, this is a different build with legal consequences for signature validity; document types that must never change are excluded from the flow.

open.question: Is something for amending signed documents already available on the platform or with your e-signature provider but not switched on?
open.would_change: If so, much of the build could be replaced by configuration.

open.question: Must the original signatories sign again, or is internal re-approval enough, and who approves the new version?
open.would_change: Re-signature adds an e-signature integration step; the choice of approver decides whether segregation of duties is respected.

open.question: Which version should people treat as current while the new version awaits approval?
open.would_change: Keeping the signed version current avoids a gap, but showing nothing until approval changes the publication logic.

open.question: Which documents are in scope, which managers may change them, and should some never be modifiable after signature?
open.would_change: A narrow scope allows a simple right; a broad one needs scoping by entity and classification.

open.question: Does signing currently trigger other actions, and should a new signature repeat them?
open.would_change: If it does, repeat-safe handling becomes part of the first release.

open.question: Is there a legal or audit obligation behind this request, and are the rules the same for every client?
open.would_change: A named obligation makes the audit trail a core deliverable; per-client variation moves the rules into configuration.

assumptions.text: The signed version is never modified in place; an edit creates a new version.
Existing versioning, approval circuits and publication are reused.
Prior signatures do not carry over automatically to the new version.
A full audit trail of who changed what and who re-approved is required.
Visibility of the new version follows the document's classification.
Managers are the people who edit and re-approve.

briefs.problem: Signed documents sometimes have to change, and today it is unclear how to do that without breaking the validity of the earlier signature or the audit trail.
briefs.solution: A controlled 'revise a signed document' path: a manager starts a new version from the signed one, it goes through approval and fresh signature, and it replaces the old version as current while the signed original stays frozen and retrievable.
introduces: a supersession flow that creates a new version from a frozen signed one
a re-approval and re-signature circuit, with rules on who may approve their own edit
a 'current version' rule separate from 'approved', so readers always know which version to act on
an audit trail covering who changed what, why, and who re-approved
re-trigger handling for downstream automation fired by signature events
permission rules for who may start a revision, tied to classification

challenges.headline: Editing signed documents at all
challenges.premise: Managers should be able to 'edit' a document that has already been signed.
challenges.alternative: Treat every change as a new version that supersedes the signed one. The signed original is never altered, and the new version is approved and signed in its own right. This keeps the earlier signature valid for the content it covered, and the history can be shown intact.
challenges.consequence: A true in-place edit breaks the link between a signature and the content it was given on, and leaves the audit trail unable to show what was actually signed. It is hard to defend later and expensive to retrofit.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means 'issue a new version' before anything is designed. If they really want in-place changes, take that to compliance first.

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: A new capability is needed for editing and re-approving signed documents.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has versioning, approval circuits and publication. The request may be covered by switching on or configuring supersession for signed documents, with a modest extension for re-signature.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel flow duplicates the approval circuits and creates a second definition of 'current version' that readers and other modules can confuse.
challenges.recommendation: Have a lead engineer walk the existing versioning and approval flow with a signed test document before estimating anything. Record the gaps, not the whole feature.

challenges.headline: One flow for every change
challenges.premise: Any change to a signed document follows the same edit, re-approve and re-sign path.
challenges.alternative: A typo correction, a genuine change of terms and a periodic renewal carry different risk. A lighter path, such as a reason code and a single approver, could cover corrections, while changes of terms get full re-signature.
challenges.consequence: A single heavy path gets bypassed through workarounds outside the system for small fixes. A single light path undermines signature validity for material changes.
challenges.recommendation: Ask the client which kinds of change they actually need, and design the first release around the one or two that matter most.

complexity_reasons: supersession must keep the signed version frozen and referenceable
re-approval circuit with separation of duties
ambiguity between approved, published and current
audit trail and retention with no gaps
briefs.cost_driver: re-approval and re-signature circuit design, and keeping the current-version rule unambiguous
risks: People acting on the wrong version while the new one is in review, or after it is approved but not yet published.
Signatures invalidated or re-collected without the people involved being told, or a signatory who has left blocking the circuit.
Re-signing re-triggering downstream automation (activation, invoicing, notifications) and creating duplicates.
Links, citations and other modules that point at the old version going stale or pointing at the wrong one.
Permissions on drafts and superseded versions left until acceptance testing, when they depend on classification and are cross-cutting.

opportunities.text: Reuse the existing versioning and approval circuits for a general 'supersede a frozen document' flow, rather than a signed-document special case.
Apply the same supersession pattern to contracts and amendments, so a change to a signed contract and a change to a signed document share one mechanism.
Make the re-approval circuit and the revision reasons configurable per client, since circuits are already client-specific.

next_steps: Confirm with the client that 'edit' means a new version that supersedes the signed one, and name the real need: correction, change of terms or renewal.
Walk the existing versioning, approval and publication flow with a signed test document to list what is genuinely missing.
Settle who re-approves and re-signs, whether the editor may approve their own change, and which version stays current during review.
Define the audit and downstream-automation requirements before estimating, so they are built in rather than retrofitted.

decisions.decision: A signed version is never changed in place; a change creates a new version that supersedes it.
decisions.why: Signature validity and the audit trail depend on the signed content staying intact and referenceable.
decisions.alternative: Allow in-place edits of signed documents.
decisions.tradeoff: More steps for the manager, in exchange for a defensible history and valid signatures.

decisions.decision: Approval and signature are kept separate from publication, so the old version remains current until the new one is approved and published.
decisions.why: Readers keep a clear current version during review.
decisions.alternative: Withdraw the old version as soon as a revision starts.
decisions.tradeoff: Two versions exist for a while, in exchange for no gap where nothing is current.

decisions.decision: An audit trail of who changed what, when and who re-approved is part of the first release.
decisions.why: Editing signed documents is audit-sensitive, and retrofitting an audit trail is expensive.
decisions.alternative: Add the audit trail in a later phase.
decisions.tradeoff: More work up front, in exchange for no gaps in the history.

page.title: Revising signed documents safely
page.recommendation: Decide what 'edit a signed document' should mean. We recommend that a manager starts a new version from the signed one, that it goes through fresh approval and signature, and that it replaces the old one as current only once approved. The signed original stays untouched and retrievable.
page.why: Changing a signed document in place breaks the link between the signature and what was signed, and leaves the history unable to show it. A new version keeps both intact. The platform already handles versions, approval circuits and publication, so the work is probably an extension of what exists rather than a new system.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is designing the re-approval and re-signature circuit, and keeping 'which version is current' unambiguous. The risk that matters most is people acting on the wrong version, or re-signing re-triggering automation that already ran for the first signature.

open.question: What is the real need: correcting a mistake, a genuine change of terms, or a renewal? And which document types are involved?
open.would_change: A typo-level correction could use a lighter path with one approver, while changes of terms need full re-signature. The document types set the scope.

open.question: How is a signed document changed today, and does the platform already have versioning or e-signature that covers part of this?
open.would_change: If most of it exists, the work shrinks to configuration and a small extension.

open.question: Who must re-approve and re-sign, and may the manager who made the edit also approve it?
open.would_change: It defines the approval circuit and separation of duties, and could add a compliance or higher-level approver.

open.question: While the new version is in review, should readers keep seeing the old signed one as current?
open.would_change: If the old one must be withdrawn immediately, we need a gap-handling rule for what readers see in the meantime.

open.question: Which managers may start a revision, and should that differ by client?
open.would_change: Per-client rules make the behaviour configurable instead of standard, which raises the build effort.

open.question: Is there a compliance, audit or electronic-signature obligation, and does signing trigger anything downstream?
open.would_change: A named obligation makes the audit trail and retention central to the build, and downstream triggers need rules so they do not fire twice.

assumptions.text: 'Edit' means issuing a new version that supersedes the signed one, never changing the signed one in place.
Earlier signatures do not carry over: the new version must be approved and signed again.
Existing versioning, approval circuits and publication can be reused.
An audit trail of each change is required.
This is a feature for known internal users on the existing platform, paid for by the client.

briefs.problem: Signed documents sometimes need to change, and there is no stated way to change them and have the change re-approved without losing the validity or history of what was signed.
briefs.solution: A supersession path on the existing document platform: a manager starts a new version of a signed document, it goes through re-approval (and re-signature where required), the signed version stays frozen and retrievable, and the whole history is recorded.
introduces: a 'supersede signed document' flow that creates a new version from a frozen one
a re-approval circuit distinct from the original, with editor/approver separation rules
a rule for which version is current while a replacement is pending
re-signature collection, possibly from external signatories
handling of references and downstream subscribers that point at the superseded version
audit entries linking each new version to the signed one it replaces

challenges.headline: Editing signed documents at all
challenges.premise: Managers need to edit documents after signature, and re-approval is enough to make the change valid.
challenges.alternative: Treat the need as 'issue a new version of a signed document'. The signed version is never edited; a successor is created and approved or re-signed. Where the need is only a small, pre-agreed change, a lighter amendment-style path keeps the original intact and avoids full re-signature of the whole document.
challenges.consequence: Literal in-place editing would break the signatures on the original and leave a gap in the audit trail. Treating every edit as a full re-signature may be needlessly heavy if most changes are corrections.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client that an edit means a new version and not an in-place change, and find out what share of changes are corrections versus renegotiated terms before sizing the re-signature work.

challenges.headline: Managers approving their own edits
challenges.premise: The managers who edit are also the natural people to re-approve.
challenges.alternative: Require the re-approver to be someone other than the editor, for instance a higher level or the original approvers, so that a change to signed content is always reviewed by a second person.
challenges.consequence: If the editor can approve their own change, a signed document can be altered and re-validated by one person, which is exactly what an auditor would look for.
challenges.recommendation: Decide the re-approver and the editor/approver separation rule before designing the circuit.

challenges.headline: Which version is live meanwhile
challenges.premise: 'Edit and re-approve' implies one document that simply moves through states.
challenges.alternative: Keep the signed version as the current one until the new version is approved and published, then stamp the old one as superseded. Approval and publication stay separate steps.
challenges.consequence: Without a stated rule, people may act on a draft or on an outdated version, and re-approval may re-fire signature-triggered automation twice.
challenges.recommendation: Settle which version is current during review, and whether re-approval counts as a new signature event for downstream modules.

complexity_reasons: builds on existing versioning, approval circuits and signature handling, so it is an extension
two lifecycles (approval/signature and publication) must stay consistent
reconciling references and downstream subscribers to the old version
briefs.cost_driver: the re-approval and re-signature circuit, including what happens to anything pointing at the old version
risks: People acting on a superseded version if 'current' is not clearly defined and visible.
Signature validity: prior signatures must not be carried over silently, and the rule for what needs re-signing is not yet known.
Downstream automation triggered by signature may fire again on re-approval and duplicate actions.
The shared access-control and classification layer may need extending, and permissions are often discovered late.
Audit trail gaps: the history of who changed what and who re-approved is hard to retrofit, and any legal hold or retention rule may block the change.

opportunities.text: Build one generic 'supersede a frozen version' capability, rather than a signed-document special case, so the same mechanism serves any approved or signed content.
Make the re-approval circuit configurable per client by reusing the existing approval circuit engine rather than creating a second one.
Expose supersession as an event so subscribers can reconcile references to the old version.

next_steps: Confirm with the client that an edit creates a new version, and agree the reason behind the request and the document types in scope.
Check whether the existing versioning, approval circuits and signature handling already cover most of this, before sizing any build.
Define the re-approval rules: who re-approves, who must re-sign, editor/approver separation, and which version is current meanwhile.
Specify audit and retention requirements and the behaviour of downstream subscribers, then derive acceptance scenarios.

decisions.decision: An edit after signature creates a new version; the signed version is frozen, retained and stamped superseded once the successor is published.
decisions.why: Signed content must stay intact and referenceable, and in-place editing would invalidate signatures and the audit trail.
decisions.alternative: Editing the signed document in place.
decisions.tradeoff: More process (a new version and re-approval each time) in exchange for preserved signature validity and a clean history.

decisions.decision: Managers are the role that can start an edit of a signed document.
Every change is recorded in a full audit trail linking the new version to the one it replaces.
decisions.why: Altering signed documents is what an auditor examines, and retrofitting an audit trail later is expensive.
decisions.alternative: A lighter change log added later.
decisions.tradeoff: Some extra up-front build work in exchange for no gaps at audit time.

page.title: Editing signed documents safely
page.recommendation: Decide whether 'editing a signed document' means issuing a new version that is re-approved, rather than changing the signed document itself. We recommend building a supersession path on the existing platform: a manager starts a new version, a second person re-approves it (with re-signature where required), the signed version stays frozen and retrievable, and the full history is recorded.
page.why: Changing a signed document in place would break its signatures and leave a gap in the record, which is exactly what an auditor would examine. Your platform already has versioning, approval circuits and signature handling, so a new-version path is likely an extension of what exists rather than a new system, and it keeps one clear answer to which version people should act on.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is the re-approval and re-signature circuit, together with reconciling anything that points at the old version. The risk that matters most is people acting on an outdated version, or signature-triggered automation firing a second time when the new version is approved.

open.would_change: If most edits are small corrections, a lighter amendment-style path could replace full re-signature and reduce the build.

open.would_change: If an existing tool covers it, we would configure or buy rather than build.
